author: rknop
body:
Fixed the problem where zogy subtractions was shifting the flux around.  This is verified with a new test `tests/improc/test_zogy.py::test_zogy_positioning`.

The issue had to do with where zogy expected the PSF to be centered (and we weren't quite meeting that expectation).  It was a little bit mysterious, and probably has to do with numpy's `fftshift` and which pixel it expects the 0 frequency to show up on.  (See comment in `improc/zogy.py::zogy_subtraction`.)

In order to fix this, I removed zogy's custom padding routine, and refactored zogy to take a PSF object instead of an image of the PSF.  I then added a method to PSF that gives you a centered image-size PSF image... with an optional offset so that zogy could put it where it wants it.  I also had to clean up the psfex rendering a bit so that it was consistently placing things offset by half a pixel.  (Because of rounding conventions and even vs. odd numbers, it was sometimes going one way, sometimes the other...!)  To test all this, I needed to add a delta function and gaussian PSF, and then because of this refactor, I needed to add an image PSF to use with the simulator and zogy tests.  Rather than have lots of if statements in lots of functions (which is what we usually do when there are different formats or algorithms for some kind of object), I refactored PSF to have subclasses, which meant learning about SQLAlchemy polymorphism (which, for this use case, turns out to be pretty straightforward).

As a side effect, I also modified the image simulator so that you could pass in a random seed, allowing it to be repeatable.  This is a gratuitous addition to this PR.  Originally, I thought I was going to use it in my new tests, but the simulator is way too heavyweight for what I needed.  But, when I thought I was going to do that, I really didn't want to write more flaky tests.  So, as a nice side effect, we no longer have to mark a bunch of zogy tests as flaky that we used to have to mark as such.

As a side effect to the side effect, I started wanting to see the output of some simulator tests, and i so doing I refactored a bit what `INTERACTIVE` means when running tests.  (Guy didn't run in a docker environment, so could show plots interactively.  I wanted to make plots without showing the interactively, so `INTERACTIVE` wasn't enough.  I split it into `MAKE_PLOTS` and `INTERACTIVE`.)

### Description
Fix `build.gradle` script not to use `true` as a default AVX settings.
Currently, we have three AVX settings as listed below:
 - AVX2
 - AVX512
 - AVX512-SPR

The issue is, regardless of whether if Linux environment supports the settings, since we are assigning the variable with `System.getProperty("...", "true")` which return "true" when it is not set, `gradle` always passes `-DAVX512_SPR_ENABLED=true` even for an instance not having the Intel SPR process installed.

This always force `make` to link `avx512-spr` shared library due to the `if-else` evaluation order in cmake file - [Code](https://github.com/opensearch-project/k-NN/blob/main/jni/cmake/init-faiss.cmake#L125)
It first evaluates whether OS is Windows, then check whether AVX512_SPR_ENABLED is set which is always true.

This is only issue in Linux environment, and due to this, KNN operations always fails as it could not find avx2 so file or avx512 so file for non-SPR processor. 

Hence, fixing `build.gradle` to pass AVX related parameters to `cmake` only if when user configured manually.

# User Model Improvements
## Move Methods to Policies/Services/Queries, Objects and Concerns

### What?
This PR moves user methods related to password Validation from the user model to a new user concern called `PasswordValidations`.
This also moves the related test from the user_test to the new `password_validations_test` concern test.

### Why?
The complexity and size of the User model have become an obstacle to any feature work that involves user-related logic. Rails concerns offer an alternative way of organising code within a single model and help to manage complexity by encapsulating a trait of the host model into a cohesive unit.
